title: From Search Tool to
AI Talent Intelligence Platform
redrob-llm.brief: Transforming a Recruiter Search Platform into an AI-Powered Professional Workspace.

cover.label: Redrob AI — From Search Tool to Talent Intelligence Platform

redrob-llm.overview: Redrob began as a single-purpose people-search tool and evolved into a connected, AI-native prospecting platform — spanning People Search, Company Search, a self-serve Developer Hub, and Redrob AI, a fully conversational LLM interface.

problemStatement.intro: The product had a single functioning feature — People Search — designed to help recruiters discover and enrich candidate profiles. This created four interconnected challenges:

challenges.v: Recruiters relied heavily on complex filter combinations to find relevant candidates, making the experience time-consuming and cognitively demanding. It required excessive manual effort before users could achieve meaningful results.

The platform was built around People Search, while customer needs had expanded beyond candidate discovery. Recruiters increasingly wanted to explore target companies and integrate Redrob into their existing workflows through APIs.
The recruitment industry was rapidly shifting toward AI-assisted experiences, where users expected to express hiring intent in natural language instead of manual filters.

problemStatement.closing: The challenge was to improve the core search experience, expand the product ecosystem with new capabilities, and increase feature adoption through better discoverability.

redrob-llm.businessGoals: The objective was to evolve Redrob from a feature-centric recruiter search tool into a scalable, AI-powered Talent Intelligence platform — and to strategically reposition Redrob for its next phase of growth.
myRoleDetail: Owned the UX strategy behind the platform evolution.
Started with auditing the existing product, running feedback loops with users and internal sales teams.
Translated findings into measurable improvements at every stage.
Defined the vision for how the product will scale with the future roadmap.
targetAudience: Founders & small-team operators doing their own outbound prospecting
Recruiters sourcing candidate pools by role, skill and company

phases.name: Optimizing the Core Experience of People Search
triggers: The results interface lacked clear hierarchy.
There was no quick way to capture user feedback.
High-value business data was not monetized effectively.
research: Conducted a UX audit, treating myself as a user.
Collected and analysed feedback from recruiters, sales teams, and internal stakeholders.
Ran a competitive analysis of Juicebox, Apollo, Clay, and Lusha.
decisions: Expanded search filters — decision makers, growth intent signals, separated funding and revenue signals.
Improved the results interface by clubbing action items and simplifying the UI.
Introduced feedback mechanisms — quick feedback popups and ratings.
Introduced premium filters — moved high-value filters like revenue and advanced decision-maker targeting into paid plans.

outcomes.k: Faster time to first relevant profile

phases.name: Introducing Company Search
triggers: Users were frequently switching between Redrob, LinkedIn, company websites, and Google to gather organization-level insights before identifying the right people to contact.
This workflow increased research time and caused users to lose context while moving between multiple platforms.
research: Benchmarked comparable workflows of Apollo and Lusha to understand established mental models.
Observed that after finding a company, the next immediate task was identifying decision-makers and relevant employees.
Designed the underlying People ↔ Company relationship model in collaboration with engineering, so the two entities felt like one connected graph rather than two separate tools.
decisions: Shipped a standalone Company Search with advanced filters (industry, headcount, funding, tech stack).
Built a Company Detail Profile page summarising key account data at a glance — size, HQ location, founded year, industry.
Added a bi-directional pivot — jump from a company to its people, and from a person's card back to their company — inside a single connected flow.

outcomes.k: Increase in cross-feature adoption between Company Search and People Search
Retention by enabling end-to-end research within a single platform

phases.name: Developer Hub — API Keys
triggers: Enterprise and agency prospects were asking for programmatic access.
There was no dedicated experience for developers to generate and manage API keys, monitor usage and credits, track enrichment requests, or access documentation.
research: Interviewed technical stakeholders, in-team developers, and enterprise prospects to understand integration expectations.
Ran a competitive analysis of developer platforms such as FullEnrich and Apollo API to understand what's important and how to showcase it.
Mapped the core flow: Generate API Key → Read Documentation → Integrate API → Monitor Usage → Track API Logs.
decisions: Designed a self-service Developer Hub with API key generation and rotation.
Built a usage dashboard surfacing credits consumed, rate limits, and call history in real time.
Added API logs & status tracking — endpoint, request method, timestamp, contact info, enrichment status, webhook status, error messages.

outcomes.k: Reduction in API onboarding time through self-service docs & guided setup

phases.name: Redrob Chrome Extension
triggers: Recruiters spent significant time sourcing candidates on LinkedIn before switching to Redrob to enrich contact details and manage prospects.
This constant context switching fragmented the workflow: copy LinkedIn profile → open Redrob → search the same profile → enrich contact details → add to list.
research: Learned that users weren't searching directly inside Redrob — LinkedIn was their primary discovery platform, while Redrob was used for enrichment and contact discovery.
Mapped the ideal workflow: Browse LinkedIn → View Redrob Insights → Add Prospect → Auto Enrich → Sync to Redrob.
decisions: Designed a lightweight side panel that appears directly on LinkedIn profile and company pages, so users can access Redrob insights without leaving their workflow.
Enabled one-click capture of any LinkedIn profile — the extension auto-fetches profile data and prepares it for enrichment instead of manual copy-paste.

outcomes.k: Increase in prospects added to Redrob lists

phases.name: Reimagining Search with AI Query & Prompt Library
triggers: The rapid adoption of conversational AI had fundamentally changed user expectations.
Users no longer wanted to build searches manually — they wanted to simply describe what they were looking for.
research: Ran comparative usability tests — filter-first vs. prompt-first flows — with think-aloud protocols across new and existing users.
Prototyped a natural-language input that parses free text into structured, still-editable filters, preserving user trust and control.
Designed a hybrid experience supporting both interaction styles instead of replacing filters completely.
decisions: Made the prompt bar the primary entry point on People and Company Search, with manual filters kept as a visible, editable fallback rather than removed.
Parsed queries into transparent filter chips so users could see and correct exactly what the system understood.
Introduced a Prompt Library with categorised, role-specific examples (recruiter, SDR, founder, growth) users could insert and edit directly.

outcomes.k: Reduction in manual filter interactions for new users

phases.name: Redrob AI — A Fully Conversational, LLM-Based Platform
triggers: The rapid adoption of LLMs such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini had fundamentally changed user expectations.
Users expected AI to understand natural language, reason across multiple datasets, and provide answers instead of requiring manual navigation.
research: Partnered cross-functionally with AI/ML and Product to define a conversational information architecture that could hold context across turns.
Designed how structured data (people/company cards, tables) renders legibly inside a chat-shaped interface — it could not become a wall of text.
decisions: Built an MCP-based search architecture allowing users to enable different data sources before initiating a search.

Designed a conversational search experience — instead of manually selecting People Search or Company Search, users simply describe their objective, and the AI interprets intent, selects the appropriate sources, applies relevant filters behind the scenes, and returns structured results.

outcomes.k: Faster time to discover relevant people and companies
User engagement through conversational, context-aware interactions

title: AI-powered creative platform that unified 30+ fragmented image editing workflows into one intelligent workspace.
phot-ai.brief: Phot AI enables creators, marketers, and businesses to generate, edit, enhance, and publish visual content using AI. As Product Designer, I led the end-to-end UX—from research and information architecture to interaction design and design system—to simplify complex AI workflows into a seamless creative experience.

research.h: Before defining the experience, I wanted to understand how creators currently approached AI-assisted design and where their workflows were breaking down.

bullets.v: Founders, performance marketers, creative leads, e-com operators
Tracked full creative cycle: brief → shoot → edit → publish → iterate
Canva, Adobe Firefly, Midjourney, DALL·E, Pencil, Smartly, Predis & more

insights: 55% of creative angles brands test fail — not because the product is bad, but because angle selection is based on gut feel, not competitive signal data.
Creative fatigue is the #1 silent ROAS killer: CTR drops 47% on average within 2 weeks, but most brands only notice when ROAS has already declined 32%.
Performance marketers — not designers — are the primary users. The interface had to work for someone who can't distinguish a hex code from a font weight.
Listing quality on Amazon/Shopify was bleeding conversion silently: 1:1 listings-to-format ratio, unoptimised titles, and A+ content taking 5+ hours per SKU to produce manually.

problem.h: Creators and businesses spend significant time switching between multiple AI tools to complete a single creative task.'.
problem.b: This fragmented workflow increases production time, introduces unnecessary complexity, and makes AI adoption difficult for non-designers.
problem.statement: Create impactful creatives in less time

journey.h: From product URL to campaign-ready creatives, guided by signal — not guesswork.
journey.b: I mapped the end-to-end journey for a performance marketer — from inputting a product to deploying validated creatives. The critical insight from journey mapping: the biggest drop-off wasn't in production, it was in the gap between creative output and performance feedback. Brands produced creatives, published them, waited 2 weeks, then started over. The platform needed to collapse that loop.

phases.name: Input
tasks: Upload product image or paste listing URL
System auto-extracts attributes, audience context, category benchmarks
phases.pain: Manual briefing was inconsistent — different marketers described the same product in completely different ways

phases.name: Discover
tasks: AI analyses top-performing creatives in your category
Generates ranked angles mapped to your ICP
Surfaces 12+ testable angles with predicted performance scores
phases.pain: Angle selection had always been subjective — marketers were uncomfortable trusting a ranked list they couldn't verify

phases.name: Generate
tasks: AngleLab produces static, video, carousel, and story variants
ListingLab creates Amazon/Shopify titles, bullets, A+ content
VideoLab generates video ads with AI CMO and Creative Strategist agents
phases.pain: Output quality varied by product category — reflective surfaces and food photography were consistently harder

phases.name: Review
tasks: Brand consistency check against stored guidelines
phases.pain: No collaboration layer meant review happened over WhatsApp screenshots — context was always lost

phases.name: Deploy
tasks: System flags fatigue and surfaces next angle to test
phases.pain: Post-publish performance data never fed back into the creative process — every new brief started from zero

process.h: 5 sprints. Tested with live brand assets and real campaign data — not stock photos.
process.b: I ran 5 two-week design sprints, each producing a testable prototype. A non-negotiable rule: every usability test used participants' actual product images and real campaign data, not generic photos. This immediately surfaced the edge cases that matter — complex backgrounds, multi-product shots, reflective packaging, lifestyle images. Five rounds, 40 participants, 220 tasks logged. Two critical pivots emerged: the Angle Discovery interface required a transparent score explanation to build trust, and the listing editor needed a side-by-side 'before/after' view to make AI edits defensible to clients.

artifacts.v: AngleLab / ListingLab / VideoLab — 3 distinct modules, 1 unified system
Ranked angles with signal source explanations — built for non-analyst trust
5 agents: AI CMO, Creative Strategist, VideoLab, Copywriting, Human Review
Side-by-side before/after with SEO score, readability grade, CVR prediction
In-platform review with threaded comments, approval states, version history
60+ components, dark + light modes, optimised for data-dense dashboards

solution.h: Three engines. One platform. Signal-driven creative from input to outcome.
solution.b: The shipped platform has three flagship modules. AngleLab: input a product, get 12+ ranked ad angles derived from real competitive signal — not guesses. ListingLab: AI-generated Amazon and Shopify listings (titles, bullets, A+ content) produced in minutes not days, with SEO optimisation and CVR scoring built in. VideoLab: AI-produced video ads powered by a 5-agent pipeline (AI CMO Agent, Creative Strategist, VideoLab Agent, AI Copywriting Agent, and Human Review for final QA). The platform also offers a fully-managed AI Agency tier for brands that want outcomes without touching the tools.
highlights: AngleLab — AI analyses your category's top-performing creatives, generates 12+ ranked angles mapped to your ICP, and flags fatigue so you always have the next test ready.
ListingLab — Amazon and Shopify listings generated at scale: titles, bullets, A+ content, and 8+ product photos, cutting production from 5+ hours to minutes per SKU.
VideoLab — AI CMO Agent defines positioning, AI Creative Strategist writes hooks, VideoLab Agent produces visuals, AI Copywriting Agent writes the script, Human Review finalises quality.
Signal Closed Loop — performance data from live campaigns feeds back into Angle Discovery, making every cycle faster and more accurate than the last.
Dual delivery model — SaaS for teams who want control, fully-managed AI Agency for brands who want outcomes with no operational lift.

gallery.cap: AngleLab — signal-based angle discovery and creative generation
Angle ranked view — ICP-mapped with signal source transparency
ListingLab — AI Amazon listing: title, bullets, A+ in minutes
VideoLab — 5-agent AI pipeline with human QA layer
Team collaboration — review, comment, approve in-platform
Signal loop — performance data feeds back into next angle cycle

metrics.sub: Across D2C brand accounts using AngleLab
Across all customers since platform launch
Common creative workflows by combining into one
Faster testing + better creatives, verified case study

quote.q: We went from 2-week creative cycles to same-day iteration. Our design workflow is dramatically faster and more efficient.
quote.a: Nikhil Jain, Founder, Behoma — Phot AI customer

reflection.h: This project fundamentally changed how I think about designing AI-powered products.
reflection.b: I realized that users aren't looking for more AI features—they're looking for confidence that the product will help them achieve their goals without adding complexity.The real design challenge wasn't exposing advanced capabilities, but making sophisticated technology feel approachable, transparent, and reliable.

title: Designing the Official Digital
Ecosystem for a New Cricket League
bcl.brief: Designing an end-to-end mobile ecosystem for a new professional T20 cricket tournament — from live scores and fan communities to a paid Fan Ownership commerce layer.

cover.label: Big Cricket League — Designing the Official Digital Ecosystem

sections.body: Big Cricket League (BCL) launched as a new professional T20 cricket tournament featuring international legends and emerging talent. The goal was to design an end-to-end mobile ecosystem that would become the primary digital destination for cricket fans around the tournament — live scores and commentary, team and player stats, standings, news, video content — and a deeper, paid affiliation layer called Fan Ownership, where a fan can buy into a team and unlock benefits and exclusive community access.

Unlike IPL and other established cricket tournaments that have mature digital products, Big Cricket League had no official application to support fans before, during, or after matches. The absence of a centralized platform fragmented the entire fan journey. The key challenges were identified across the following areas:

items.v: Cricket fans relied on multiple third-party platforms such as Cricbuzz, Google, YouTube, Instagram, and news websites to follow a single tournament.

items.k: Lack of a Centralized Information Hub
items.v: Tournament-related information was scattered across different channels with no official source providing complete coverage.

items.k: Poor Fan Engagement Beyond Match Days
items.v: User engagement was largely limited to live broadcasts. Once a match ended, there was little reason for fans to continue interacting with the league.
The platform lacked features that encouraged fans to actively participate rather than passively consume content. There was no ecosystem for Fan ownership, Team communities, Fan loyalty.

sections.body: Rather than building another score-tracking app, the objective was to create a digital ecosystem capable of supporting the complete fan lifecycle. The platform needed to:
items: Establish Big Cricket League's own digital identity
Give all franchises a consistent home inside one platform instead of fragmented team-level presences

sections.body: With no budget in this phase for direct fan interviews, the process leaned on three inputs instead of one:

items.v: Reviewed existing league apps like IPL, Cricbuzz, cricket score/stats aggregators and fantasy platforms to establish what a strong baseline experience looks like for live score, commentary and stats.

Used well-established patterns in how sports fans actually behave — checking score compulsively during play, reacting in the moment, wanting recognition for loyalty — as design inputs in place of direct interviews.

The league's own commercial goals — sponsor visibility, and specifically the Fan Ownership commerce model — shaped scope directly and were translated into designed flows rather than emerging from user research.

sections.body: Based on insights gathered from stakeholder discussions, competitive analysis, and product research, a comprehensive Product Requirements Document (PRD) was created by the Product Manager. The PRD served as the single source of truth, consolidating business objectives, user needs, feature requirements, functional specifications, success metrics, and project scope. This ensured alignment across product, design, and engineering teams before moving into the design phase.

The sitemap organises into eight pillars, all reachable from a deliberately minimal four-item bottom navigation (Home, Fan Club, Videos, More) that pushes secondary destinations into an overflow rather than trying to surface everything at once.

table.v: Matches, Teams, Squad, Points Table, Leaderboard, Venues, News, Photo & Video Gallery, Sponsors, Founder Wall
Three distinct states — Before match (preview, prediction poll), Live (commentary, live scorecard), After match (result, full scorecard, awards) — plus Squads and Gallery per match
Overview, Squad, Matches, Fan Owners, Stats (batting/bowling leaderboards), Gallery, News, Sponsors
Overview, Awards, Badges, Polls, Equity Awards, News
Per-team fan club list, Polls, Contests (e.g. match-day selfie), Fan-Owner-exclusive wall
Become a Fan Owner, Buy & Become (benefits, terms, pricing), payment success/failure states, ownership benefits & documents
Latest Videos, Top Moments, Buzz, News, Photo & Video Galleries
4-item bottom bar — Home, Fan Club, Videos, More — keeping the primary nav simple despite deep content underneath

sections.image: User flow and annotated screens — added once final visuals are ready

sections.body: Created a prototype for each feature & shared with the developers and stakeholders to review. Feedback given was that design was very intuitive and easy to use.

title: Designing a Storytelling Platform
for an 80-Year Legacy Restaurant
pritam.brief: An immersive digital experience for one of Mumbai's most iconic restaurants — where every section tells a meaningful part of Pritam's 80-year journey, since 1942.

sections.body: Pritam Restaurant has been one of Mumbai's most iconic dining destinations since 1942, and the restaurant credited with introducing butter chicken to Mumbai. Over four generations, it built a genuine Bollywood-era legacy: Raj Kapoor inaugurated its first outlet in 1975, and many actors including Sunil Dutt, Dilip Kumar, Dharmendra and Sunil Gavaskar visited. The business now also runs Pritam Da Dhaba, a related but distinct concept with an original outlet in Dadar and a newer one in Juhu aimed at a younger audience.
sections.body2: Instead of designing a conventional restaurant website, the goal was to create an immersive digital experience where every section tells a meaningful part of Pritam's journey.

items: New visitors had no way to discover its history.
International audiences couldn't understand its cultural significance.
Customers couldn't explore its legacy before visiting.
The brand had no digital platform to preserve and communicate stories accumulated over generations.
Documented the important things to showcase
Started with moodboarding, wireframes, and design system

sections.image: Section-by-section breakdown — added once final visuals are ready

sections.body: The final product is not simply a restaurant website. It is a digital museum, a brand archive, and a storytelling platform that allows visitors to experience more than eighty years of culinary heritage before they ever step inside the restaurant.
sections.body2: By structuring the experience around stories rather than pages, the website transforms Pritam's history into an engaging digital journey while creating a scalable foundation for future growth, locations, and brand storytelling.

title: Privacy, finally
feels effortless.
pulpy-vpn.brief: Designed Pulpy VPN end-to-end from zero — a consumer privacy app for non-technical users in India and Southeast Asia. Solved the biggest unsolved problem in the VPN category: most people know they should use one and never do, because every VPN on the market was designed for IT professionals. Shipped an 88-second onboarding, a one-tap connection state designed to feel actively protective, and a paywall strategy that delivered 3.2× trial-to-paid conversion — reaching 100K+ downloads and a 4.2★ Play Store rating within 6 months.

context.h: 31% of internet users want a VPN. Fewer than 5% use one. The product category was designed for the wrong person.
context.b: The global VPN market was growing fast, but adoption in India and Southeast Asia was disproportionately low despite high demand for streaming access and growing public WiFi safety awareness. The reason wasn't price — it was product. Every major VPN (NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark) was built for a technically confident user: protocol pickers, DNS leak test dashboards, kill switch toggles, and onboarding flows that required understanding what a VPN server actually does. The typical user in our target market — college students, freelancers, working parents — had tried one, felt confused, and uninstalled. Pulpy VPN's founding insight was sharp: the market that most needed a VPN was the exact market every VPN had designed itself away from. The brief was to build the first privacy app that a person with zero technical knowledge could use confidently in under 90 seconds.

research.h: 40 people who'd tried a VPN and quit. The reason was always the same word: 'protocol'.
research.b: I led a 4-week research sprint combining qualitative depth with quantitative pattern analysis. I ran 40 interviews across two cohorts — abandonment cases (people who downloaded and uninstalled within a week) and retention cases (current VPN users who stuck with their app). I supplemented this with a moderated usability audit of 6 leading VPN apps across 20 non-technical participants, and a large-scale review analysis of 600+ app store reviews across NordVPN, ExpressVPN, and Surfshark in India and the Philippines. The gap between the two cohorts wasn't technical ability — it was emotional experience at the moment of connection.

bullets.v: 28 abandonment cases (uninstalled within 7 days) + 12 long-term retention users — across India, Philippines, Indonesia
6 leading VPN apps tested with 20 non-technical participants — tracking confusion points, drop-off moments, emotional state
NordVPN, ExpressVPN, Surfshark — India + Southeast Asia App Store reviews coded for friction, anxiety, and praise themes
Information architecture and onboarding flow maps for 8 VPN apps — identifying the 14 decision points that caused abandonment

insights: The word 'protocol' — appearing in the first screen of every major VPN — caused 78% of non-technical users to disengage entirely. They didn't know what it meant, feared selecting the wrong option, and closed the app.

The connection state was the single highest-anxiety moment in the product: users couldn't tell if the VPN was actually working. A static 'Connected' label wasn't enough. They needed to feel protected, not informed.

Non-technical users had exactly 2 use cases for a VPN — public WiFi safety and geo-restricted streaming — and didn't identify with any of the 40+ use cases that most VPN marketing presented. The category was talking to itself.

Retention users shared one trait: a moment early in their experience where the product made them feel smart, not confused. The emotional transformation from 'I don't understand this' to 'I'm protected' was the product's most critical design moment.

personas.name: Priya Venkat
personas.role: Engineering student, 21, Bangalore — frequent campus and café WiFi user
personas.quote: I downloaded NordVPN because my friend said I need it. There was a screen asking which protocol to use. I uninstalled it.
goals: Stay safe on campus and café WiFi
pains: Technical screens feel like a test she might fail
Doesn't understand 'kill switch', 'DNS leak', 'protocol' — won't guess
Fears accidentally doing something that breaks her internet

personas.name: Deshawn Reyes
personas.role: Freelance designer, 29, Manila — works remotely across coffee shops and co-working spaces
personas.quote: I need a VPN when I'm on client calls from cafés. I just want something I can turn on in 5 seconds and trust it's working.
goals: Protect client data on public networks without thinking
Reliable mid-call — no drops, no reconnects
One subscription that covers his phone and laptop
pains: Silent disconnects during calls with no warning
Monthly billing UI feels opaque — doesn't know what he's paying for

personas.name: Meena Sharma
personas.role: Working parent, 44, Delhi — non-technical, concerned about family's online safety
personas.quote: My son said download a VPN. I downloaded one. There was too much to read. I deleted it.
goals: Understand that it's working and protecting her family
Simple enough to use without asking for help
Extend protection to her kids' phones without complexity
pains: Every VPN screen is full of jargon she doesn't recognise
No visual confirmation that protection is active
Fears accidentally changing a setting that breaks something important

problem.h: Reframed from 'build a faster VPN' to 'design the first VPN that feels like safety, not IT.'
problem.b: The original brief from the founders was competitive: more server locations, faster speeds, better pricing than NordVPN. Research made clear that this was the wrong race to run. Speed and server count were table stakes — every major VPN had them. The real gap was emotional. The category treated confidence as something users had to bring to the product. Pulpy's job was to design confidence into the product itself — to make the feeling of being protected a primary design output, not a side effect of configuration. Every technical decision had to be made for the user, not by the user.
problem.statement: How might we design a VPN that makes a completely non-technical user feel genuinely safe and confident within 90 seconds — without a single technical decision, setting choice, or jargon word standing between them and protection?

journey.h: App store to protected — in under 90 seconds, with zero technical decisions.
journey.b: I mapped the full journey from app store discovery through to paid subscription renewal. The critical insight from journey mapping: there were 14 decision points in a standard VPN onboarding flow, and every single one was a potential drop-off. My design constraint was explicit from week 1 — eliminate every required decision that wasn't name, goal (why they wanted a VPN), and the single connect tap. Everything else had to be a smart default. The paywall placement was a separate journey design challenge: end-of-trial paywalls tested poorly (felt like a deadline, triggered anxiety and churn), while mid-use paywalls placed immediately after a meaningful success moment tested 3.2× better.

phases.name: Discover
phases.pain: Category is crowded — Pulpy had no brand recognition vs. NordVPN. Discovery copy had to lead with 'simple', not 'secure'

phases.name: Onboard
tasks: Tell us why you want a VPN
phases.pain: Original 7-step onboarding had protocol selection on screen 2 — 61% of users dropped here in early testing

phases.name: Connect
phases.pain: Static 'Connected' label produced high anxiety — users weren't sure if it was working

phases.name: Use
phases.pain: Silent reconnects with no notification generated the highest-volume support ticket: 'Is my VPN still on?'

phases.name: Convert
tasks: Mid-use paywall at a success moment
phases.pain: End-of-trial paywall tested as arbitrary and punitive — users who'd had a positive experience still churned at 68%

process.h: Hard constraint: under 120 seconds. 6 onboarding tests. 8 connection animations. Shipped at 88s.
process.b: I set a measurable design constraint in the first week: onboarding must reach the 'protected' state in under 120 seconds, measured by task completion time in Maze with non-technical participants. Every design decision was evaluated against this constraint. I ran 6 rounds of onboarding testing (15 participants per round), tracked time-on-task, completion rate, and a self-reported confidence score after the connected state. Round 1 was 4 minutes 12 seconds. Round 5 was 88 seconds. The biggest single gain came from removing server selection entirely in round 2 — smart auto-selection based on the user's stated goal cut 90 seconds alone. The connection animation was the highest-ROI design artefact in the entire project — 8 iterations tested, with the version that communicated 'active scanning + protection forming' producing the highest confidence scores across all user types.

artifacts.v: Reduced from 7 screens to 3: name → goal → connect. 6 testing rounds. Shipped at 88 seconds, 94% completion rate.
Lottie animation: 'protection activating' visual with shield-forming + scanning arc. Single highest-impact design decision tested.
Goal-based auto-selection (Streaming → lowest-latency international / Safety → nearest high-trust server). Removes the hardest user decision.
4 paywall placement tests — after first successful streaming session, after 5-day streak, at trial end, and immediately post-connect. Mid-use won at 3.2× vs. trial-end.
'You are protected' persistent UI — live indicator, data encrypted counter, reconnect log, network name. Designed for anxiety reduction.
Protocol, server region, DNS settings — accessible 3 taps deep. Never shown unless actively sought. Power users satisfied; new users unaffected.

solution.h: One tap to protected. Confidence by design. Everything else stays out of the way.
solution.b: The final product was built on three non-negotiable design principles: zero required decisions (every technical choice — server, protocol, DNS — is made by the system, not the user), designed confidence (the connection state was treated as a primary emotional design brief — the animation, the persistent indicator, the 'You are protected' language were all intentional outputs), and progressive complexity (power settings exist and are complete, but are only accessed by users who actively seek them — never surfaced as default screens). Onboarding is 3 screens. The core interaction is one button. Every other screen is optional.
highlights: 3-screen onboarding: name → why you want a VPN → one-tap connect. Reaches 'protected' state in 88 seconds, no technical knowledge required.
Goal-based smart server: auto-selects optimal server based on Streaming or Safety goal — protocol, region, and DNS set automatically. Zero configuration.
'Protecting you' connection animation: 8 iterations of Lottie animation — shield forming, network scanning arc. Single highest-confidence score in all user testing.
Confidence dashboard: persistent 'You are protected' UI with live data encrypted counter, reconnect log, and network name. Designed specifically to eliminate the #1 support ticket.
Mid-use paywall: placed immediately after a meaningful success moment (first protected streaming session) — not on a countdown timer. 3.2× trial-to-paid conversion vs. trial-end placement.

gallery.cap: Onboarding — 3 screens, 88 seconds, zero technical decisions
Smart server — goal-based auto-selection, no protocol picker
Confidence dashboard — live protection status, encrypted data counter
Mid-use paywall — placed after first streaming success, not on a timer
Power mode — protocol settings hidden 3 taps deep, never default

metrics.sub: First 6 months post-launch, India + Southeast Asia
App open → first protected state. Across all tested device tiers.
Mid-use paywall vs. original end-of-trial placement in A/B test
Organic reviews — highest-rated review theme: 'simple to use'

quote.q: I've tried two other VPNs and deleted both. This one — I turned it on and it told me I was protected. I didn't have to do anything else. That's the one I'm paying for.
quote.a: Beta user, working parent, Pune — post-launch survey

reflection.h: Confidence is a design deliverable. Not a feature — a designed emotional state.
reflection.b: The most important thing I shipped on this project wasn't a screen — it was the connection animation. One Lottie file, 8 iterations, and it had more measurable impact on user retention than any feature we built. It proved something I'd believed but never had data for: on a consumer product where trust is the core value proposition, the user's emotional state at the critical moment is as important a design output as any functional screen. I now define 'emotional state design' as a formal deliverable on every consumer product I work on — what does the user feel at each key moment, and is it the intentional, correct feeling? The second learning: progressive disclosure isn't just an IA technique. On Pulpy, hiding complexity made the product feel safer — and safer products convert better. I'd apply that thinking much earlier on the next 0→1 consumer product.
